docs.text: Ouroboros or-uh-bore-us Extract ROIs from cloud-hosted medical scans. Ouroboros is a desktop app (built with Electron) and a Python package (with a CLI). The desktop app uses Docker to build and run its Python server. For this reason, Docker is required to run Ouroboros. If you are interested in using the Python package for its CLI or for a custom usecase, check out the python folder in the main repository. Ouroboros also has a Plugin System . Plugin servers are also run in Docker. Usage Guide It is recommended that you read these pages in order. Download and Install Ouroboros Slicing Backprojection Plugins Reference Technical Constants - hardcoded file explorer limits and plugin broadcast behavior. Large Folder Behavior The Ouroboros File Explorer is designed to open scan and output folders directly, but it is not a general-purpose file browser. It loads subfolders on demand: opening a folder shows only that folder's direct entries, and subfolder contents stream in when you expand each subfolder. When you point it at a folder that contains many files or deeply nested subfolders, the following behavior applies: Only the root's direct entries are loaded up front. Nested subfolders are loaded and watched only when you expand them. Collapsing a subfolder keeps its state and watcher alive for a short window (thirty seconds by default) so quickly re-expanding is free. If you leave it collapsed past that window, the underlying watcher is torn down and the subfolder's cached children are dropped from renderer state; re-expanding later behaves like a fresh load. The panel stops loading new paths after one hundred thousand visible entries across all currently open watchers. When this happens, Ouroboros shows a warning toast asking you to pick a smaller folder or expand the folder in smaller pieces. node_modules , __pycache__ , venv , and any directory whose name starts with . are always skipped. See Technical Constants for the exact values, why they were chosen, and when to adjust them. Ouroboros Explanation A user of Ouroboros may have a multi-terabyte volumetric scan, hosted with the Neuroglancer family of tools (i.e. cloud-volume ). Perhaps there is a long, relatively sparse structure (ROI), like a nerve or a blood vessel that crosses the entire scan. Even with a well-equipped computer, it would be difficult to segment the entire stucture in one pass due to RAM limitations. Ouroboros provides a solution. A user first traces the structure in Neuroglancer with sequential annotation points, and then saves the JSON configuration to a file. Ouroboros opens this configuration file and cuts rectangular slices along the annotation path, producing a straightened volume with the ROI at the center of each slice (usually much smaller than the original scan). Every tenth slice in a circular annotation path, rendered in Ouroboros's Slicing Page. From there, the user segments the much smaller straightened volume with their choice of segmentation system. Then, Ouroboros backprojects the segmented slices into the original volume space (unstraightens it), producing a full segmentation.

docs.text: Development Docker and WSL troubleshooting Start with the README's Development Quick Start . It owns the installation, launch, and interactive verification sequence. This page covers backend verification and conditional troubleshooting; run commands from the repository root unless stated otherwise. Verify and rebuild the development backend Close the installed Ouroboros app and other development instances before launching. Development and installed apps share the ouroboros-server container name, ports, and ouroboros-volume volume. Do not use a running released container as evidence that the current branch is being tested. npm run dev starts both the Docker backend (port 8000) and the host volume-transfer service (port 3001). Starting Compose alone does not start that host service, which is needed to transfer inputs and deliver results. After launching, inspect the running container: docker inspect ouroboros-server --format '{{json .Mounts}}' docker logs --tail 50 ouroboros-server In the mounts, the source for destination /app/ouroboros must correspond to this checkout's python/ouroboros directory (Docker Desktop may translate the host path). The logs should show Uvicorn watching /app/ouroboros and completing application startup. If the mount is absent or points to another checkout, stop the app that owns that server and restart development from the intended checkout. python/compose.dev.yml uses the normal Python Dockerfile for dependencies, binds the checked-out package at /app/ouroboros , and enables Uvicorn reload. Source edits in that package do not require an image rebuild. After dependency or Dockerfile changes, close the development app, rebuild, then relaunch using the README sequence: docker compose -f python/compose.dev.yml build ouroboros-server Docker Desktop is running but WSL cannot connect A missing socket error such as this means the development shell cannot reach Docker: failed to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock connect: no such file or directory In Docker Desktop, enable the WSL 2 engine and Settings → Resources → WSL Integration for the specific distribution running development, then apply the changes. If integration settings are absent, check that Docker Desktop is using Linux containers. Retry docker info in the same WSL shell you use for npm run dev ; it must return server information. Docker Desktop being open, or a container running elsewhere, does not verify this connection. See Docker's WSL integration instructions . Electron uninstall after npm ci With the Electron 43.7.8 / electron-vite 5 combination tested for #141, Electron's binary was downloaded on demand, while electron-vite read Electron's path.txt directly. Thus an otherwise successful dependency installation could still end with Error: Electron uninstall at launch. Run the explicit install-electron step in the README. It uses Electron's bundled installer ; no custom downloader is needed. Check the installed executable with: npm exec --no -- electron --version This verifies executable installation, not the GUI or Docker connection. JSON paths and folder selection Paths must be valid for the operating system running Electron. Linux Electron inside WSL needs /mnt/c/... or /mnt/wsl/... , not C:\... or \\wsl$\Ubuntu\... . Native Windows Electron uses Windows paths. Use File → Open Folder , choose the containing folder, then drag the JSON from the app's file explorer into Neuroglancer JSON . The slicing page currently ignores JSON changes before a working folder has been selected, even when the typed absolute path is valid. In the GTK folder picker, Ctrl+L lets you enter an absolute folder path. Conditional X11 file-picker workaround In the session recorded in #141 , the app used a forwarded X11 display ( DISPLAY=localhost:10.0 ), but the desktop portal lacked a usable X11 display. Portal logs reported Failed to open X11 display and failure to associate the dialog with its parent. The user saw a nonfunctional window with [WARN:COPY MODE] in its title; that title alone is not a diagnosis. For this portal/X11 mismatch, close the development app and launch with: GDK_BACKEND=x11 npm run dev -- -- --xdg-portal-required-version=999 Both -- separators are intentional: npm consumes the first, and electron-vite forwards the arguments after the second to Electron. The portal-version switch selects the native GTK dialog when the portal does not meet that version requirement; GDK_BACKEND=x11 uses the app's X11 display. An actual Electron 43.7.8 folder dialog was verified with this launch. This is conditional troubleshooting, not a requirement for every WSL installation, and it does not establish that WebGL works. WebGL preview failures The slicing page's React Three Fiber Canvas in VisualizeSlicing.tsx draws the 3D slice/bounding-box preview. These repeated messages indicate that its WebGL context could not be created: THREE.WebGLRenderer: A WebGL context could not be created. GL_VENDOR = Disabled, GL_RENDERER = Disabled, Sandboxed = yes ErrorMessage = BindToCurrentSequence failed The app does not explicitly disable hardware acceleration and currently provides no preview fallback for context creation failure. A functioning file picker and successful backend processing are separate from a functioning preview. Capture the failing launch Record the launch command, Electron version, and DISPLAY , WAYLAND_DISPLAY , and XDG_SESSION_TYPE from its shell. Distinguish a WSLg session from forwarded X11; the observed localhost:10.0 was forwarded X11. Check Microsoft's WSL GUI/OpenGL prerequisites for WSLg. Capture the preview error from the renderer's DevTools console ( F12 in development) and GPU messages from the launch terminal. For Chromium logging and a main-process debugger, add --inspect before electron-vite's -- and --enable-logging after it: npm run dev -- --inspect -- --enable-logging . Retain any display settings and other Electron switches from the failing launch. Attach a Node debugger to the inspector address printed in the terminal (electron-vite 5 defaults to port 5858). In that main-process debugger, collect Electron's app.getGPUFeatureStatus() after GPU initialization ( gpu-info-update ), and app.getGPUInfo('complete') , including any rejection. These APIs belong to app from electron , not the renderer's console. Use diagnostics from the actual failing app; an isolated probe alone does not establish its GPU state. An isolated Electron 43.7.8 check on the same forwarded display reproduced WebGL2 blocklisted / unavailable_off . The exact blocklist cause and trigger for repeated preview renders remain unconfirmed; forwarded X11 is diagnostic context, not a proven cause. Verified software-rendering launch For the affected environment, close the development app and retain the working file-picker configuration while selecting the bundled SwiftShader driver: GDK_BACKEND=x11 npm run dev -- -- \ --xdg-portal-required-version=999 \ --use-gl=angle \ --use-angle=swiftshader These Chromium driver switches render on the CPU and may be slower than hardware acceleration. They apply to this launch and require no source changes. Do not use --disable-gpu or --no-sandbox as the standard fix. The isolated Electron 43.7.8 check created WebGL2 with an ANGLE/SwiftShader renderer and returned the expected pixel [255,128,0,255] . The owner subsequently confirmed that the same command worked in the actual development app. This was not warning-free : the app still printed an automatic SwiftShader fallback deprecation warning despite the explicit driver switches. The probe also logged a GPU stall from its synchronous readPixels check. The tested launch needed neither --enable-unsafe-swiftshader nor --no-sandbox ; do not add the unsafe opt-in merely to suppress the warning. The earlier eight successful Docker operations and delivered statistics verified backend/output delivery; the later owner confirmation verified the preview separately. These observations are recorded in #141 , not a claim of new GUI testing for this documentation change. A graceful preview fallback or logging change is a separate application task. Other build paths Installed apps use the server image pinned by digest in the release lock . Docker pulls a missing image; the installed app does not build a server wheel or image. Local plugin installation explicitly builds Compose after copying the plugin into the app data folder, when its new backend files become available. The plugin template uses plugins/plugin-template/backend/compose.dev.yml during npm run dev-backend , mounts backend/app , and runs FastAPI development mode. Rebuild that Compose service after dependency or Dockerfile changes; ordinary source edits use reload. The packaged backend/compose.yml stays unchanged. Keep GPU-specific containers in plugins or optional Compose overrides. The core server does not require CUDA; segmentation plugins such as SAM-backed plugins are the appropriate place for CUDA runtime bases.

docs.text: Production package flavors The release workflow builds the flavors selected by release/release-lock.json for each supported desktop runner. The available flavors are: core : Ouroboros only, with the production server compose file pointing at the registry-published server image. with-plugins-cpu : the core package plus bundled Neuroglancer and Automatic Segmentation plugin artifacts. The automatic segmentation plugin uses its CPU backend image. with-plugins-cuda : the core package plus bundled Neuroglancer and Automatic Segmentation plugin artifacts. The automatic segmentation plugin uses its CUDA backend image and Docker Compose GPU reservation. Plugin flavors stage bundled assets in separate resource directories inside the external packaging workspace. Electron Builder maps each flavor's resources into the installed extra-resources directory, including extra-resources/preinstalled-plugins . The app installs those bundled plugin folders into the user plugin directory on startup. Release inputs The release lock is the only source of production pins and selected flavors. Update it to change the server image or bundled plugins; there are no separate per-image or per-plugin workflow inputs. The application version must match the lock's releaseVersion . The server is pinned by registry repository, immutable image digest, and source commit. Plugin inputs are pinned by repository, release tag, asset filename, SHA-256, and source commit, with separate CPU and CUDA backend identities. Packaging verifies downloaded archive hashes and requires plugin-release.json to match the locked release identity. Backend image verification follows the corresponding lock entry. See the lock for current versions and digests. The packaged extra-resources/package-flavor.json records the selected flavor, release-lock hash, server image metadata, and exact plugin identities, including the verified plugin release metadata. This file describes the package; the release lock remains authoritative. If plugin release repositories are private, set OUROBOROS_RELEASE_ASSET_TOKEN to a token that can read those release assets. The workflow falls back to GITHUB_TOKEN when that secret is not set. Build and publication Pull requests run release preflight checks without building native installers. Native builds run on main , compiling Electron once per operating system and packaging each selected flavor. On CI, build workspaces, generated resources, dependency trees, plugin downloads, and final artifacts live under RUNNER_TEMP , outside GITHUB_WORKSPACE ; the source checkout is read-only input. Electron Builder uses an explicit application-file allowlist rather than packaging the checkout. Source files and installed dependencies are copied once into an external tree where Electron is compiled. Every flavor packages that same compiled application and dependency tree, with npmRebuild: false enforced. Flavor preparation and cleanup affect only that flavor's resources and output directory. The shared compiled tree remains available across flavors and is removed at the end of the run; there are no links back to checkout dependencies. A successful main build records the exact source commit, input lock, artifact sizes, and SHA-256 hashes. The tag-triggered publication workflow verifies those prebuilt artifacts and creates a draft release without rebuilding Electron or the server. See the release pipeline guide . Dependency auditing uses npm run audit:release against locked dependencies. Any reviewed audit exceptions are defined in the audit validator . Local checks Run the fast release preflight from the repository root: npm run preflight:release It validates the lock, application version, and packaging configuration, and exercises disposable external staging without compiling Electron, downloading plugin assets, or producing installers. Build all locked flavors on the corresponding native platform: npm run build:release-artifacts -- --platform linux Use mac on macOS or win on Windows. Scratch files and final artifacts default to RUNNER_TEMP , or the operating system's temporary directory when running locally without that variable. The command prints the final output location. Set OUROBOROS_RELEASE_ARTIFACT_DIR to choose another destination beneath that temporary root. It must be an absolute path outside the checkout and must be new or empty; existing artifacts are not cleared. Scratch files are removed after the run, while final artifacts are retained. The existing build:linux , build:mac , and build:win commands use the same staging and packaging entrypoint. For a local single-flavor build, select a flavor already present in the lock, for example: OUROBOROS_PACKAGE_FLAVOR=core npm run build:linux npm run build:unpack creates an unpacked application for the current platform through that entrypoint and prints its external location. Preparation and renaming scripts are internal build steps, not standalone checkout commands. Plugin downloads use the workspace's cache. To seed it with local release archives, set OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_DIR to an external directory that does not overlap the checkout or build inputs and outputs. Its contents are copied into the owned workspace cache; the original directory is never modified. Copied archives must match the filenames and SHA-256 values in the release lock. Stale copies are replaced within the workspace, without changing the originals or overriding the locked plugin identities.

docs.text: Registry Server Images The Python server image has a separate build lifecycle from desktop installers. Production packages use the image digest pinned in release/release-lock.json , so application startup pulls the image instead of building it locally. Published Image The Build and Certify Server Image workflow tests Python changes, builds the wheel, and builds python/Dockerfile-prod on pull requests. PR runs do not publish an image. On main , the workflow publishes sha-<full-commit> and records the registry repository, image digest, and source commit in a certified server manifest. docs.text: Shared-memory ownership python/ouroboros/helpers/mem.py owns shared NumPy allocation, attachment, serialization, and release. Its lifecycle handling adapts lftomo/util/mem.py at 8d4c884 : non-owning serialization, cleanup guards, and manager cleanup after owner death. Ouroboros does not import lftomo's role-based reuse planner or storage interfaces; there are no consumers of those facilities here. Allocation and handoff The manager server's shared_memory_context is the sole registry of managed allocations. Each entry contains a live SharedMemory handle and the allocation's release policy. The prior global termed-name list and its proxy are removed. The standard library's names-only tracker is replaced, not maintained alongside the owning registry. list_segments derives its answer from that registry. SharedNPArray() and TermedNPArray() allocate through the same server RPC. The server establishes ownership before returning a name. The client opens a local attachment and constructs array views; failed client attachment or view construction releases the server allocation. Inherited ShareableList() registration also opens an owning server handle before acknowledging the client. Serializing SharedNPArray transfers only its name, original shape, dtype, and view description. Deserialization opens a non-owning attachment; it does not transfer unlink authority or cached NumPy data. The server keeps the buffer alive even if the producer exits before the consumer opens it. This matters on Windows, where the allocation disappears when its last handle closes. Release and failure handling Run-scoped arrays and standard manager allocations live until manager shutdown. Termed arrays are released by remove_termed() at the existing per-volume completion point in VolumeCache.remove_volume() . They do not accumulate until shutdown. Validation and owner release are atomic at the server; an unknown or run-scoped name is rejected without closing the supplied array. On POSIX, release unlinks the name and closes the manager's handle. Already-open attachments remain valid until they close; new attachments cannot open the name. On Windows, release closes the manager's handle. Existing attachments keep the allocation alive until they close. The supplied array, when present, is closed after the server acknowledges release. Closing a deserialized attachment never unlinks the creator's allocation. Explicit array cleanup is idempotent and handles partial construction. Normal manager shutdown uses SharedMemoryServer.shutdown() and that same owning registry. A client-side shutdown() override would be replaced by BaseManager.start() 's finalizer and is not used for allocation cleanup. The manager detaches from the owner's POSIX process group, as in lftomo, so it can clean up after that group is killed. A watcher waits on Python's parent-process sentinel on all supported platforms; owner death releases tracked allocations and exits the manager. POSIX SIGTERM to the manager also triggers cleanup. Forcibly killing the manager itself cannot execute its cleanup code; Windows closes its handles, while POSIX retains its standard resource-tracker fallback. The server tracker and startup hooks depend on CPython manager internals. Native CI exercises Python 3.11 and 3.12 on Linux, Windows, and macOS. Tests prove producer exit before receiver attachment, per-buffer release, surviving mapped consumers, serialization authority, failed construction, normal/exception shutdown, and owner termination. Multiprocessing coverage includes the live server code. Before raising the Python upper bound in python/pyproject.toml , re-check these three CPython interfaces against every newly supported version: BaseManager._run_server and startup/finalization: the mirrored signature, parent-process sentinel, and replacement of the client shutdown() method. multiprocessing.managers.dispatch : request signatures and the server's exception-to- RemoteError conversion used by the release-result adapter. SharedMemoryServer.shared_memory_context : the tracker interface consumed by allocation registration, listing, release, and server shutdown. None of the platforms adds a separate resident TIFF-cache term; ordinary mapped-file pages can still contribute through their process counters. See memory measurements for metric names, platform requirements and remaining semantic differences. Process and allocation changes invalidate an in-progress sweep. Persistent publication failure invalidates the report's memory coverage without changing scientific allocation behavior. docs.text: Status presentation This document is the presentation reference for slicing, backprojection, and the autoseg plugin. It defines display semantics, not backend states or readiness rules. Each repository maps its existing observations at render time. Do not store the mapped values as another execution or connection authority. Display status Meaning Appearance Waiting A step is pending or an expected observation is awaited. Neutral Running The source reports that work is active. Blue Complete The source reports successful completion of this step. Green Warning A reported condition needs attention; it does not establish task failure. Amber Failed The source explicitly reports failure of the named operation. Red Interrupted The source explicitly reports interrupted execution. Red Unknown The available observation does not establish the state or outcome. Neutral Use Complete , not Succeeded or Completed, on state labels; use Failed , not Error, for an operation's state. Sentences can say “Slicing completed.” Notice severity ( info , success , warning , error ) describes a message, not execution state. Contextual labels such as Connected or Loads on first run are appropriate when they describe the actual observation more precisely than a generic state. Main-app step values pending/running/succeeded/failed/interrupted map to Waiting/Running/Complete/Failed/Interrupted . Autoseg's pending/in_progress/completed/error/warning normally map to Waiting/Running/Complete/Failed/Warning . These are display adapters; wire values stay unchanged. A known source-specific meaning takes precedence over blindly translating a string: autoseg's lazy ML-runtime warning means the model is not loaded yet, so it uses neutral Loads on first run , not a startup failure. The backend summary and checklist show separate observed facts. In the main app, launch-command completion does not establish backend readiness. A reachable backend plus a failed local launch displays Connected — local launch failed , with Failed on the launch row and Connected on the connection row. With no local launch observation, omit that row. Do not create additional probes to fill out a checklist. Autoseg's backend and browser volume observations must be named separately, since they can disagree. Task percentages describe their reported stages. They do not establish the overall outcome. Show the reported terminal result independently of notice dismissal. Communication trouble or a missing job does not establish Failed; preserve existing last-reported information and identify an unknown outcome where already observed. Keep workflow-specific stages rather than inventing a universal lifecycle. The main app's STATUS_LABELS and StatusLabel own its display vocabulary and state appearance. Plugin views follow this document through their local display adapter. A shared cross-repository runtime package is not required. Notices Use compact notices beside the information they explain: launch diagnostics in the initialization section; submission, task, and communication diagnostics in the task section. Keep the reported text and failure-stage details, including statistics-report messages. Long paths and messages wrap, and explicit line breaks remain readable. Severity uses a subdued background and border with these accents: info #a9ceff , success #a7ddb5 , warning #f3d18b , error #ffb3a8 . Errors announce with role="alert" ; other notices use role="status" . A request diagnostic has a visible, keyboard-accessible Dismiss button. Reported outcomes, steps, launch observations, and communication warnings remain source-derived and do not disappear when that diagnostic is dismissed. The main app moves only task-start request failures ( /slice/ , /backproject/ ) and previous-task deletion failures into these retained notices. Local form/input errors (including invalid options and Neuroglancer JSON), filesystem warnings, and rendering errors keep their existing global alerts. A moved failure is not also shown as a toast. ServerContext remains the owner of request errors; there is no copied notice history or page-local dismissal flag. Dismiss clears only that request's error, preserving results, pending state, and task/stream data. A new submission clears its earlier start and deletion notices before preparing the request. Successful requests retain their existing error-clearing behavior. Input editing or an unrelated successful request does not clear a retained diagnostic. Unlike autoseg's error list, these notices follow the existing request lifecycle rather than accumulating past failures. Undismissed errors retain the existing provider lifetime and can still be seen on returning to a page. A dismissed error cannot reappear on navigation because it was cleared at its owner. No navigation/reload storage is added. Each deletion request is identified by its actual task-specific URL ( /delete/?task_id=… ), so one workflow cannot display another workflow's deletion failure. The saved task response remains the source of that task ID until the existing deletion/submission lifecycle replaces it.

docs.text: Backprojection After straightened volume produced by the slicing step is segmented, Ouroboros's Backproject Page can be used to project the segmentation back into the coordinate space of the original volume. Using the Backproject Page Basic Usage Demo Reusing Options from a Previous Run See the same section under Slice Page . Compression Options One of the options on the Backproject page allows the user to configure the output compression format. Common options zlib zstd none (no compression, not recommended) For more information, see Tifffile , the Python package responsible for the compression. Output Position Offset By default, the slicing output tiff image is backprojected into the space of its minimum bounding box, rather than the space of the entire source scan. The offset of the minimum bounding box is stored in the output tiff's description metadata. It is also stored in the configuration file (which is modified by the backproject step). Output File Name - Base name for all output files. Output MIP Level - The MIP level to output the backprojection in (essentially an upsample option). Use this if you downsampled in the slicing step; downsampling changes are currently ignored. Upsample Order - The interpolation order Ouroboros uses to interpolate values from a lower MIP level. If you check the binary option, feel free to set this to 0. Backprojection Compression - The compression option to use for the backprojected tiff(s). Recommended options: none , zlib , zstd . Output Single File - Whether to output one tiff stack file or a folder of files. Performance Logging - Off by default. Enable to save detailed performance statistics beside the outputs. Progress bars and step timings remain available when off. The setting is saved with your options; older options files without it load with logging off. The saved preference applies to desktop runs; CLI runs require --verbose regardless of the saved preference. Output Min Bounding Box - Save only the minimum volume needed to contain the backprojected slices. The offset will be stored in the -configuration.json file under backprojection_offset . This value is the (x_min, y_min, z_min). Binary Backprojection - Whether or not to binarize all the values of the backprojection. Enable this to backproject a segmentation. Offset in Filename - Whether or not to include the (x_min, y_min, z_min) offset for min bounding box in the output file name. Only applies if Output Min Bounding Box is true. Process Count - Number of parallel processes to use during the backprojection process. Reducing count will slow process but decrease memory usage; at default chunk size each process tends to approximate 0.5 GB in usage. Chunk Size - Size of each dimension (x/y/z) of the processing chunk. Increasing will increase memory usage; performance is a more complex tradeoff and making it too large will negatively affect performance. How Does Backprojection Work? A large amount of helpful data is saved in *-configuration.json file after the slicing process. This data contains all of the rectangle corners from slicing, and the bounding boxes the slices are associated with. With this data, Ouroboros recalculates the 2D coordinate grids of 3D points for each slice. Trilinear Interpolation Backprojection iterates through 3D chunks of the straightened volume, as follows following order: The chunks are loaded from a memory map of the straightened volume. A custom rapid trilinear interpolation implementation is used to map the slice data into a sparse representation of the backprojected volume, limited to a bounding box containing only points associated with the chunk. These sparse representations are written to disk intermediates, with individual files for each slice of the backprojected volume they are associated with. As chunks are completed, it evaluates which slices of the backprojected volume can be fully written by completed chunks. The data for these slices are loaded from the intermediates, then written to disk in the target folder as they are completed. Once all slices are completed, they are converted to a single file if this configuration option is enabled. Why Is Interpolation Needed? The slices in the straightened volume were originally produced through interpolation. Each slice has a 2D grid of 3D points, and the values at these points were approximated through interpolation. In order to put the data back, we have to interpolate in the opposite direction. Each point contributes to the value of its neighbors based on how close it is to them.

docs.text: Ouroboros Plugins Recommended Plugins Neuroglancer Plugin Embeds Neuroglancer as a page in the app. Supports loading from and saving to JSON configuration files in Ouroboros's File Explorer. Has additional features like fullscreen mode and screenshots. Assisted Automatic Segmentation Plugin Coming Soon! Based on Segment Anything, it attempts to automatically segment the ROI. Benefits from the assumption that the desired structure is centered in each slice. Supports human input via bounding boxes and positive or negative annotations. Installing a Plugin Open the Plugin Manager: File > Manage Plugins . Press the Plus Icon Paste the GitHub URL of the plugin. Press Download (Ouroboros downloads and installs the plugin for you) Where are plugins installed? In the appData /ouroboros folder. This folder is different on each OS. Preinstalled Production Plugins Production packages can bundle plugin folders under extra-resources/preinstalled-plugins/<plugin-name>/ . On startup, Ouroboros copies missing bundled plugins into the normal user-data plugin folder before it loads plugins. Bundled plugin installs are idempotent and version-aware. If a user already has the same plugin installed, Ouroboros compares the version field in each plugin's package.json ; it upgrades only when the bundled version is newer and skips existing installs that are current, newer, or not safely comparable. Creating a Plugin See the template README for more information. Directory Context in Plugin Iframes When Ouroboros posts a send-directory-contents message to plugin iframes, the payload contains the selected directory's directoryPath and directoryName but the nodes field is always an empty object. This broadcast fires on every root change and is intended as a notification only — plugins should not depend on receiving the full recursive file tree through it. To read the directory tree, plugins request it explicitly with the request-directory-contents message described below. Requesting Directory Contents Plugins ask the provider for the entries of a folder (optionally recursive) by posting a request-directory-contents message. The provider replies with a send-directory-contents-response message addressed only to the requesting iframe. Request (plugin → provider): window.parent.postMessage( { type: 'request-directory-contents', data: { path: '/absolute/path/under/current/root', recursive: true, // optional; defaults to false requestId: 'abc-123' // optional; the provider echoes it back } }, '*' ) Response (provider → requesting iframe): window.addEventListener('message', (event) => { if (event.data?.type !== 'send-directory-contents-response') return const { path, nodes, requestId, error } = event.data.data // `nodes` is a path-keyed nested map of { name, path, children? } // matching the shape the pre-#106 broadcast used. // `error` is present only when the request could not be fully served: // - code: 'denied' path outside the current root, or no root open // - code: 'not-found' path does not exist / is not a directory // - code: 'limit' enumeration hit the aggregate cap; `truncated: true` // and `nodes` holds the partial result // - code: 'internal' unexpected error; see `message` }) If requestId is omitted from the request, the provider generates one and echoes it back on the response so plugins can still correlate. Path-traversal guard. Requests for paths outside the current root are rejected with code: 'denied' . Plugins get exactly what the user can see in the File Explorer and nothing above it. Truncation. When the aggregate visible-path budget ( FILE_EXPLORER_WATCH_LIMIT ) is exceeded mid-walk, the enumeration stops and the response is returned with error.code: 'limit' , error.truncated: true , and a partial nodes map. Callers issuing recursive requests on very large trees should be prepared to handle this. Ignore rules. The same ignore filter the File Explorer uses (dotfiles and the node_modules , __pycache__ , venv segments) applies here. Plugins cannot bypass it. For details and the values behind other file explorer limits, see the Technical Constants reference.

docs.text: Slicing Slicing is one of the primary features of Ouroboros, available in the CLI and the desktop app. Using the Slice Page Basic Usage Demo Reusing Options from a Previous Run Slicing Options 📁 - Drag and drop files from File Explorer panel into this option. 📁 Neuroglancer JSON - Path to the Neuroglancer configuration JSON file (exported from Neuroglancer with {} icon, or through the Neuroglancer Plugin) Neuroglancer Image Layer - Select Neuroglancer image layer to slice from. Neuroglancer Annotation Layer - Select Neuroglancer annotation layer to slice from. Slice Width - The output width of each slice image. Slice Height - The output height of each slice image. 📁 Output File Folder - The folder to save all the resulting files into. Output File Name - Base name for all output files. Annotation MIP Level - The annotation layer's MIP level. 0 is the highest resolution. Output MIP Level - The MIP level to output slices in (essentially a downsample option). 1 is a good starting point. Slicing Parameters Distance Between Slices - The distance between each slice along the annotation path. Use Adaptive Slicing - Rather than just using equidistant slices, add more slices in more curved areas. Adaptive Slicing Ratio - 1 indicates to consider distance and curvature equally, 0.5 is biased towards distance, and 2 is biased towards curvature. Output Single File - Whether to output one tiff stack file or a folder of files. Performance Logging - Off by default. Enable to save detailed performance statistics beside the outputs. Progress bars and step timings remain available when off. The setting is saved with your options; older options files without it load with logging off. The saved preference applies to desktop runs; CLI runs require --verbose regardless of the saved preference. Bounding Box Parameters Max Depth - The maximum depth for binary space partitioning. It is not recommended to change this option unless you encounter RAM issues. Target Slices Per Box - If you are running on a low-RAM system, or you are taking very large slices, you may want to decrease this. How Does Slicing Work? Spline Fitting Ouroboros fits a spline curve to the annotation path from the Neuroglancer JSON file. This produces a smooth, differentiable curve along the length of the annotations. If the line segments between annotation points were used, then there would could be highly discontinuous slice transitions around sharp corners. Slice Coordinate Frames Ouroboros calculates equidistant points along the spline curve. Each point is "1" apart from the previous to match the appearance of isotropic slices taken from one of the axes of the coordinate space of the full volume (the coordinate space of the annotation points). To follow any possible path, each point must have its own coordinate frame normal to the spline. For easier segmentation, it is also important that the axes of the point coordinate frames don't flip between points. To achieve this, Ouroboros calculates rotation-minimizing frames based on the change in orientation of the tangent vectors of adjacent points. Rectangles and Grids Ouroboros calculates the corners of the slice rectangle at using each point and its associated coordinate axes (as vectors). Pseudocode width_vector # 'u' unit vector scaled to slice width / 2 height_vector # 'v' unit vector scaled to slice height / 2 top_left = point - width_vector + height_vector top_right = point + width_vector + height_vector bottom_right = point + width_vector - height_vector bottom_left = point - width_vector - height_vector Then, for each point, a 2D grid is generated with given dimensions (slice width and height). Each point in the 2D grid is a 3D point which is calculated by interpolating between the four corner points. Volumes and Trilinear Interpolation At this point, Ouroboros has a full grid of 3D points associated with each slice, but has yet to download any data from the cloud-hosted volume. To avoid downloading unnecessary data, Ouroboros employs binary space partitioning to divide the minimum bounding box of the ROI recursively until each volume contains few enough slices to fit into available RAM. Ouroboros then downloads the data for each of these bounding boxes from the cloud-hosted volume. As each download completes, a new process is spawned to handle calculations. For each volume, scipy.ndimage.map_coordinates is used to extract the values at the coordinates of the slice grids from the 3D volume using trilinear interpolation. Each of these slices are saved as local tiff images and are later combined into a single output tiff.

docs.text: Pipeline run statistics Use --verbose with either Python CLI operation to print and save the same formatted statistics JSON: ouroboros-cli slice slice-options.json --verbose ouroboros-cli backproject backproject-options.json --verbose The report is written beside the configured outputs, using <output_file_name>-<operation>-<run_id>-statistics.json . Each invocation gets a new run identifier, so repeated runs retain their reports. This works with a single TIFF or a directory of TIFF planes. JSON numeric values retain their precision; byte counts are integers. Console headings and progress bars are outside the JSON payload. Without --verbose , the CLI skips the pipeline's accumulation of detailed timing samples, memory sampler, volume statistics, report formatting and report writes. Existing worker phase clocks still run; basic step duration and progress remain available. The pipeline factory's verbose argument continues to control its progress bar; it is separate from run reporting. Server and Docker Server tasks report statistics by default. Pass reporting_enabled=false to POST /slice/ or POST /backproject/ to disable detailed reporting for that task. Both CLI and server use the same operation lifecycle and reporting code. The existing status response and status events include statistics : { "status": "published", "path": "/configured/output/sample-slice-run-id-statistics.json", "recovery_path": null, "error": null } Publication status is pending , published , disabled , unavailable , failed , or interrupted . The API keeps a task active through required cleanup and publication; duplicate submission and deletion remain blocked while it is active. Cleanup remains part of that lifecycle when reporting is disabled. A progress read failure is exposed as progress_error without changing the scientific outcome. Docker copies scientific outputs to the host and cleans its working folder before finalizing the operation timer. It then stages and transfers the report through the existing volume server into the configured host output directory. Reports retain private file permissions ( 0600 on POSIX). For Docker exports on POSIX hosts, the volume server assigns the copied report to its host user and group so that user can read it. Windows retains Docker Desktop's host mapping. Undelivered reports are retained under /volume/main-statistics/ , outside the scientific working folder. The status response gives the recovery path. Successful delivery removes the staging copy. Normal operation and desktop shutdown cleanup preserve undelivered statistics; explicitly deleting the Docker volume also deletes those recovery copies. Scientific outcome and report-publication outcome are distinct. A failed scientific-output transfer makes the operation fail. A failed statistics write or transfer leaves a successful scientific outcome intact but exposes the publication error through status, an error event, and server logging. A console or log presentation failure is exposed separately as presentation_error ; an example is BrokenPipeError when a consumer such as head closes stdout while --verbose prints the saved report. presentation_interrupted distinguishes an interruption during this final output. Neither changes the scientific outcome or an already-published file's delivery status and path. The CLI exits with status 1 on failure and 130 on interruption, including interrupted report delivery or presentation. When options cannot be loaded and no output destination is known, the report is explicitly unavailable; no report is silently written to the current directory. Desktop status presentation The slicing and backprojection progress panels show scientific outcome and statistics publication separately. A completed task retains its final progress when report delivery fails, is interrupted, or is unavailable. The panel shows a reporting warning with the publication error and any recovery location; an unpublished path is labeled as the intended destination. Only published identifies a delivered report. Disabled reporting produces no missing-report warning. A scientific failure or interruption appears first, even when its statistics report was delivered successfully. The HTTP/SSE contract is unchanged: /status/{task_id} can return HTTP 500 with status: done , and a stream can emit error_event for successful science with a reporting problem. The desktop interprets the validated status and statistics descriptor, rather than treating the event name or aggregate error as the scientific outcome. For failed/interrupted science the aggregate error retains Task.error priority; publication and log-presentation errors are displayed separately from that descriptor. No report files are read to reconstruct status. Publication pending keeps the server status active and retains the existing submission/deletion guards. Terminal status closes its stream; events for other task IDs and events from closed/replaced streams are ignored. Connection failures or invalid status payloads close the stream and show a communication warning with the last reported progress, without declaring a scientific failure or resubmitting the task. Status messages remain in the progress panel until the stream is cleared or a new task starts, so a recovery location does not disappear with a timed alert. The existing unknown-task response ( status: error , error: Item ID Not Found , and no statistics descriptor) is also treated as an outcome-unknown warning. The stream closes and retains the last reported progress: the backend may have restarted or dropped the task, which does not establish scientific failure. This exact legacy response is recognized at the stream boundary; other scientific errors retain their normal presentation and the API contract is unchanged. The narrow identity adapter in common/memory_ipc.py serializes the validated private Process._ident value together with the psutil version and platform. It matches incoming identities against live Process objects at the IPC boundary; serialized values do not become a second runtime identity registry. Missing, unsupported, or unverified identity data makes the affected measurement unavailable rather than falling back to a PID or public creation timestamp, or treating an unverified manager as owning no segments. Psutil is pinned to 7.1.3 in package metadata as well as the Poetry lock, covering pip/wheel installations and both Docker build paths. This private-API dependency must be reviewed before changing that pin: Linux, Windows and macOS identity/IPC compatibility tests and the clock-adjustment regressions must pass for the proposed version. Supported runtime identity comes from psutil itself; Ouroboros does not maintain an alternative platform identity calculation. Liveness checks likewise validate a fresh psutil identity before comparing it with the retained Process : unreadable identity is unknown coverage, not proof that the worker exited. Discovery still uses psutil's children() implementation; in 7.1.3 a backwards clock adjustment within one enumeration can omit a previously unseen child because psutil itself filters by public creation timestamps. Retained workers are checked independently, but sampling is not a complete process census. status is sampled when all admitted sweeps succeeded, partial when some failed, unavailable when none completed, or not_started if the pipeline was never reached. Process or allocation changes during a sweep make that sweep incomplete. Manifest reads and publication reuse the control-file retry for Windows sharing violations (up to 0.5 seconds, 10 ms spacing). Persistent failures remain explicit. A failed manager-manifest publication invalidates the metric rather than silently omitting managed allocations. The peak is the maximum complete sampled tree total , not an OS high-water mark or a sum of independently observed process peaks. Reads within a sweep are sequential, not an atomic tree snapshot. Sampling may miss short-lived peaks; external processes sharing pages affect Linux PSS. Sweeps crossing the end of the operation are discarded. Requested and observed intervals, sweep cost, complete and incomplete counts and errors accompany the result. No complete sample means an unavailable value, never a successful zero. The default interval is one second; collection cost is assessed against combined reporting overhead. last_complete_sample_bytes is the last admitted complete sample, not a live reading at report publication. sampling gives the window length, first and last admitted sweep offsets, requested interval, observed start-to-start interval range, and discarded/incomplete/complete counts. collector_cpu_seconds includes polling and completion of an in-flight sweep discarded at stop; max_sweep_seconds includes discarded sweeps too. These costs diagnose the observer; only an external pipeline timer measures in-operation overhead. The native CI matrix covers Linux, Windows and Apple Silicon macOS on Python 3.11 and 3.12. The current simplification is checked with focused ownership, accounting and reporting tests; it has not repeated the long real-data benchmark campaign. Historical Linux and Windows pipeline results, component diagnostics, and Docker/frozen-executable checks are retained in the Python benchmark guide . Those results describe earlier collectors. In particular, the earlier Windows long-path overhead finding applies to the removed working-set enumeration and mapping-tracking implementation, not a measurement of this replacement. Focused tests do not establish a 1% overhead bound or native macOS pipeline acceptance. No cross-platform 1% guarantee is claimed. The clock-dependent identity defect in #162 invalidates the affected RAM results; fixing identity does not retroactively repair those reports. Fresh long-run overhead acceptance is tracked separately in #163 , and replacement publication measurements remain under #121 . The native macOS pipeline and macOS-host Docker deferrals on #139 remain unchanged.

docs.text: Technical Constants This page documents hardcoded implementation limits that affect Ouroboros behavior at runtime. Values here are extracted directly from the shipping source. If you change them locally, update this page in the same commit. File explorer All file explorer limits live in src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts at the top of the file, alongside the shared teardown delay in src/shared/constants.ts . They apply to the per-directory non-recursive watchers with lazy expansion that back the File Explorer panel in the Electron app. Starting with #110 , the file explorer no longer opens a single recursive watcher on the selected root. Instead, the main process keeps one non-recursive watcher per directory the user has currently expanded, plus one for the root. Expanding a subfolder starts a new watcher for it; collapsing schedules teardown after COLLAPSE_TEARDOWN_DELAY_MS , so quick collapse-then-reopen costs nothing. Watcher path-count limit Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_WATCH_LIMIT Value: 100_000 Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 9 Reported inside every folder-contents-error payload. Why it exists. Every watcher mirrors its discovered paths into renderer state. Even with lazy expansion, an aggressive user could open a handful of dense subfolders in sequence and still exhaust memory. One hundred thousand visible paths is the ceiling picked in [#104][pr-104] as a balance between usefulness for typical scan/output folders and keeping the renderer well under its default 4 GB heap. Role change from #110. Before #110 this was the underlying watcher package's per-watcher limit . Under the lazy model it is instead an aggregate session budget summed across every currently open watcher; a watcher's contribution is reclaimed when its folder is collapsed and torn down. Second role from #111. The same constant caps the plugin-facing get-folder-contents one-shot enumeration used by the request-directory-contents iframe message (see the plugins guide ). A plugin's recursive walk stops when the enumeration hits the cap; the response is returned with error.code: 'limit' and error.truncated: true , and nodes holds the partial result already gathered. Enumeration and watcher budgets are counted separately (the enumeration count is per-request and does not accumulate across requests), so a plugin cannot starve the file explorer by issuing many recursive requests. User-visible behavior when reached. Once the aggregate visible add count crosses the limit, the main process emits folder-contents-error with a message of the form File explorer stopped loading after 100000 visible paths across all open folders. Choose a smaller folder or expand the folder in smaller pieces. The existing renderer alert system surfaces this as a warning toast. Further add events for that session are not attributed to the counter but already loaded paths remain visible. When to reconsider. Raise this only after profiling shows headroom in both the main watchers and the renderer heap for your typical workload. Lower it if you routinely work on constrained machines and want the warning to appear sooner. Watcher teardown delay after collapse Symbol: COLLAPSE_TEARDOWN_DELAY_MS Value: 30_000 (milliseconds) Source: src/shared/constants.ts Why it exists. Collapsing a folder in the file explorer should not immediately close its watcher and drop its renderer state, because users routinely collapse-then-reopen the same folder while navigating. The delay makes that pattern free: as long as the user re-expands within thirty seconds, no watcher churn and no state re-fetch happen. After the delay elapses, the main process closes the non-recursive watcher on the collapsed subfolder and the renderer prunes its children from state. Root's watcher is exempt - collapsing root is a no-op; root's watcher only closes when a new root is opened or the window is torn down. User-visible behavior when reached. Nothing visible changes at the moment of teardown. The collapsed folder's shell remains rendered; its children have already stopped rendering visually because of the collapse. Re-expanding after teardown behaves like a fresh expand: the main process starts a new watcher and streams the initial batch back into the renderer's state. When to reconsider. Shorten if renderer memory pressure from still-cached collapsed subtrees is a problem. Lengthen if users complain that re-opening a folder after a long detour repopulates it visibly. Update batch size Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_UPDATE_BATCH_LIMIT Value: 500 Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 10 Why it exists. [#105][pr-105] introduced batching so that a large initial folder scan no longer produces one IPC message and one React state update per discovered path. Five hundred events per batch amortizes the IPC round-trip and lets the renderer apply the whole batch inside a single setNodes call. User-visible behavior when reached. As soon as five hundred watcher events have accumulated in the main process, the pending queue is flushed immediately over the folder-contents-update-batch IPC channel instead of waiting for the flush interval below. The File Explorer panel then updates once for the whole batch. When to reconsider. Increase the batch size if profiling shows IPC or React reconciliation is still the bottleneck on very large folders. Decrease it if you see visible latency between file system changes and the first batch appearing in the panel. Update flush interval Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_UPDATE_INTERVAL_MS Value: 100 (milliseconds) Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 11 Why it exists. The batch flush also runs on a timer so that small bursts of changes still reach the renderer promptly, even when the five-hundred-event threshold above is never hit. User-visible behavior when reached. Any queued events are flushed at most one hundred milliseconds after the first event in the queue was enqueued. The panel therefore feels responsive to individual file create/delete events while still coalescing large scans. When to reconsider. Shorten the interval if the panel feels laggy during light file activity. Lengthen it if renderer CPU during heavy scans is a problem and you would rather trade responsiveness for throughput. Plugin directory broadcast Broadcast payload: { directoryPath, directoryName, nodes: {} } Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/IFrameContext.tsx ( broadcastDirectoryContext ) Why it exists. Before [#106][pr-106], every directory context change posted the full recursive nodes tree into each plugin iframe. For the same large folders that motivated [#51][issue-51] this cloned the entire file tree on every update and stacked on top of the watcher and renderer costs above. User-visible behavior. Plugins still receive the selected directory path and name through the existing send-directory-contents message. The nodes field is present for shape compatibility but is always an empty object. Plugins that need to browse the directory tree use the request-directory-contents / send-directory-contents-response message pair added in [#111][issue-111] (see the plugins guide ) rather than depending on this broadcast payload. When to reconsider. Do not restore the full-tree broadcast without first landing a memory-safe, on-demand alternative. The on-demand API from #111 is that alternative; prefer extending it over resurrecting the broadcast. Main process (Electron) Plugin file server port Symbol: PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT Value: 3000 (default) Source: src/main/servers/file-server.ts line 7 Environment override: OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT (integer; unset, empty, or non-numeric values fall back to 3000 ) Why it exists. The main process forks a local Express + serve-static worker (see resources/processes/file-server-script.mjs ) that serves every installed plugin's static assets over http://127.0.0.1:3000/ by default. The renderer and plugin iframes load their index.html , icons, and any bundled JS from this server. User-visible behavior. If another process on the host is already listening on the chosen port the fork fails and plugins load with broken assets. There is no automatic fallback beyond the env override. When to reconsider. Set OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT when 3000 conflicts with a different local service. The renderer discovers the URL through getPluginFileServerURL() , so the port change is picked up without touching any user-facing setting. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. Docker volume server port Symbol: VOLUME_SERVER_PORT Value: 3001 (default) Source: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts line 7 Environment override: OUROBOROS_VOLUME_SERVER_PORT (integer; unset, empty, or non-numeric values fall back to 3001 ) Why it exists. The volume server is a second forked Node process (see resources/processes/volume-server-script.mjs ) that shells out to docker run --rm commands so that host files can be copied into and out of the ouroboros-volume Docker named volume. The main server container reaches back to it through http://host.docker.internal:3001 (see Python server below). User-visible behavior. Copy-to-volume and copy-to-host requests fail if the chosen port is busy or if Docker is not available. Plugin data transfer into the shared volume breaks in that case. When to reconsider. Set OUROBOROS_VOLUME_SERVER_PORT when 3001 conflicts locally. Keep the Python-side default in sync ( VOLUME_SERVER_URL in python/ouroboros/common/volume_server_interface.py ); the Python side is still hard-coded to 3001 because the container reaches the host over host.docker.internal where the port is independent of any host-side conflict. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. Docker volume name Symbol: VOLUME Value: 'ouroboros-volume' Source: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts line 9, matched by the volumes.ouroboros-volume.name entry in python/compose.yml , python/compose.dev.yml , and the compose file written by scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs . Why it exists. The Python server, the volume server helper, and the main process all address the same Docker named volume so that plugin uploads land where the pipeline can read them. Invariant. The literal string 'ouroboros-volume' is duplicated across four call sites: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts , python/ouroboros/common/volume_server_interface.py , python/compose.yml , python/compose.dev.yml , and the compose file written by scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs . Docker Compose YAML is required to be static, so a single source of truth would need a code-generation step the team has not opted into; the invariant lives in this documentation and in code review discipline. If you rename this value in one place, every listed file must move with it in the same commit. User-visible behavior. On app shutdown the volume server helper issues docker run --rm ... rm -rf /volume/* against this named volume. Anything else stored under the same volume name is deleted. When to reconsider. Rename it if you need to run multiple Ouroboros installs against the same Docker daemon without stomping each other's volumes. All call sites listed above must agree. Renderer Server connection settings Symbols: DEFAULT_SERVER_URL , retryDelay Values: DEFAULT_SERVER_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:8000' retryDelay = 5000 (milliseconds) Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/ServerContext.tsx lines 4 and 41 Why it exists. DEFAULT_SERVER_URL is the base URL the renderer uses for all REST and SSE calls to the Python server. retryDelay is the interval at which the checkServerStatus loop pings that base URL to update the connected flag driving the ProgressPanel status. User-visible behavior. The "connected" indicator can lag reality by up to about five seconds. Any fetch or stream started while the app thinks the server is down is placed on fetchQueue and replayed once the health poll flips to connected . When to reconsider. Lower retryDelay for a snappier connection indicator at the cost of extra HTTP traffic. Change DEFAULT_SERVER_URL if you point Ouroboros at a remote server, but keep it aligned with the Python-side HOST / PORT defaults documented below. IFrame plugin allowed origins Symbol: allowedHostnames Value: ['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '0.0.0.0'] Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/IFrameContext.tsx line 30 Why it exists. The renderer only dispatches read-file , save-file , and register-plugin messages from iframes whose event.origin parses to a URL whose hostname is exactly one of these values. Plugin content is served locally through the plugin file server (see PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT , default port 3000), so all legitimate origins are loopback. Any port on those hosts is accepted; the port itself is env-configurable. Security note. The previous implementation used text.startsWith(item) , which would accept attacker-controlled hosts such as http://localhost.evil.example . The current implementation parses event.origin with new URL(...) and compares hostname for exact equality; malformed origins fall through to a deny. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. User-visible behavior. Any plugin iframe served from a non-loopback origin is silently ignored: its messages never trigger file reads, writes, or registration. When to reconsider. Add an entry only if you deliberately host plugin content off-device (for example, over https:// to a controlled host). Broadening this list widens the file-read and file-write surface exposed to third-party pages, and non-loopback additions should use exact origin equality against a full URL, not just a hostname. Slice visualization sampling ratio Symbol: SLICE_RENDER_PROPORTION Value: 0.008 Source: src/renderer/src/routes/SlicesPage/SlicesPage.tsx line 26 Why it exists. The 3D slice preview draws only every Nth rectangle where N = floor(rects.length * 0.008) . This keeps very long paths (tens of thousands of rects) from stalling the WebGL scene. User-visible behavior. For a 10 000-rect path this renders roughly 125 rectangles: enough to convey the shape of the sweep without freezing the visualization. Fewer rects than about 125 render every rect. When to reconsider. Raise it to see more slices in the preview at the cost of frame rate; lower it if the preview lags on very long paths. Python server Server host and port Symbols: HOST , PORT , DOCKER_HOST , DOCKER_PORT Values (defaults): HOST = '127.0.0.1' PORT = 8000 DOCKER_HOST = '0.0.0.0' DOCKER_PORT = 8000 Source: [ python/ouroboros/common/server.py ][py-server] lines 10-14 Environment overrides: OUROBOROS_SERVER_HOST -> HOST OUROBOROS_SERVER_PORT -> PORT (integer) OUROBOROS_DOCKER_SERVER_HOST -> DOCKER_HOST OUROBOROS_DOCKER_SERVER_PORT -> DOCKER_PORT (integer) Why it exists. The desktop-only server entry point ( ouroboros-server ) binds Uvicorn to loopback, while the containerised server entry point ( ouroboros-docker-server ) binds to all interfaces so the host can reach the container through the compose 8000:8000 port mapping. User-visible behavior. The renderer's DEFAULT_SERVER_URL above assumes port 8000. Changing PORT (or OUROBOROS_SERVER_PORT ) or the compose port mapping without updating the renderer breaks the client. When to reconsider. Set the env overrides if you need to expose the desktop server to another machine (rare) or if 8000 conflicts with another service. Update DEFAULT_SERVER_URL in the renderer and the compose port mapping in the same commit. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. Volume server URL (Python side) Symbols: VOLUME_SERVER_URL , PLUGIN_NAME Values: VOLUME_SERVER_URL = 'http://host.docker.internal:3001' PLUGIN_NAME = 'main' Source: python/ouroboros/common/volume_server_interface.py lines 3-4 Why it exists. From inside the server container, the volume server running on the host is reached through the Docker special DNS name host.docker.internal , mapped in each compose file via extra_hosts: - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway" . PLUGIN_NAME is the fixed subfolder on the shared volume used by the main pipeline. Why 'main'. Ouroboros is the main application of its own plugin ecosystem, so the Python side treats itself as the always- main plugin when addressing paths on the shared volume. There is no planned per-plugin path scheme on the Python side; plugin content is scoped by the Electron-side plugin folder, not by a Python-visible slug. PLUGIN_NAME therefore stays a constant rather than a parameter. User-visible behavior. If the compose file omits the host.docker.internal extra host, or if the Electron main process is not running the volume server, requests time out and plugin/data transfer into the volume fails. When to reconsider. Change the URL only in coordination with the Electron-side VOLUME_SERVER_PORT in src/main/servers/volume-server.ts . Backprojection chunk and process defaults Symbols: chunk_size and process_count on BackprojectOptions Values: chunk_size = 160 process_count = os.cpu_count() Source: python/ouroboros/helpers/options.py lines 77-78 User override: fields of the same name in the backproject options JSON Why it exists. chunk_size is the per-dimension size of the processing chunk used by the backproject pipeline (see DataRange(FPShape.make_with(0), FPShape, FPShape.make_with(config.chunk_size)) in python/ouroboros/pipeline/backproject_pipeline.py ). process_count sets the parallel worker pool for the same pipeline; executor and writer processes are derived as fractions of it ( process_count // 4 * 2 or // 4 * 3 ). Why 160 specifically. The primary purpose of the chunk sizing is to enable clean backprojection - specifically clean backprojection of the flattened xyz stack. 160 is the judgment-call result for the best combination of memory and speed on standard pieces of data. Additionally, as for efficiency operations are performed on a flattened chunk, large values can cause significant slowdown and memory explsion due to change in the index bit size. User-visible behavior. Large chunk_size reduces per-chunk overhead but raises peak memory per worker and can cause disproportionate increases in memory usage and slowdowns. On very small hosts, process_count = cpu_count() may over-subscribe and thrash; lowering it in the options JSON trades throughput for stability. When to reconsider. Tune per-run through the backproject options JSON. Edit the defaults only if a different global tuning is measured to be better across typical workloads. Volume-cache flush default Symbol: FLUSH_CACHE Value: False Source: python/ouroboros/helpers/volume_cache.py line 13 User override: flush_cache field on CommonOptions in python/ouroboros/helpers/options.py Why it exists. Controls whether the cloud-volume cache is flushed after each pipeline run. Keeping it off keeps downloaded chunks around for the next run. User-visible behavior. With the default off, repeated runs against the same source volume reuse locally cached tiles, which can hide upstream data changes but greatly speeds re-runs. When to reconsider. Set flush_cache: true in the options JSON for one-shot runs or when the upstream volume may have changed. Docker and packaging Server container shared-memory size Symbol: shm_size Value: 64gb (default) Source: python/compose.yml line 15, python/compose.dev.yml line 28, and the compose file written by scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs (line 58) Environment override (packaging time): OUROBOROS_SERVER_SHM_SIZE (read by scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs and by the ${OUROBOROS_SERVER_SHM_SIZE:-64gb} substitution in both compose files) Why it exists. shm_size is an artificial Docker limit. Without a shm_size override, Docker aggressively caps container /dev/shm at 64 MB , which the pipeline exceeds immediately. Setting it too large does not "cause" OOM: it just shifts OOM from the container-side artificial limit to actual host OOM. The FastAPI server uses shared memory for inter-process numpy arrays ( SharedMemoryManager , SharedNPArray in python/ouroboros/helpers/mem.py ) and for cloud-volume caches, so the container is given 64 GB of tmpfs headroom by default. User-visible behavior. On hosts with less than 64 GB of RAM plus swap, Docker still accepts the setting ( /dev/shm is a tmpfs and allocates on demand), but attempts to actually use that much shared memory will trigger the host OOM killer. On high-RAM hosts you can raise the ceiling; on conservative shared hosts you can lower it to prefer the artificial limit hitting first. When to reconsider. Set OUROBOROS_SERVER_SHM_SIZE at packaging or runtime (compose reads the same variable via ${OUROBOROS_SERVER_SHM_SIZE:-64gb} substitution in both python/compose.yml and python/compose.dev.yml ). Lower it on constrained hosts where you know the pipelines you run stay well under the limit; raise it only if you routinely see shared-memory ENOMEM errors from the server. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. Server image reference defaults Symbols: imageRepository , imageTag Values: imageRepository (default) = ghcr.io/chenglabresearch/ouroboros-server imageTag (default) = v${packageJson.version} (falls back to GITHUB_REF_NAME in CI) Source: scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs lines 10-14 Environment overrides: OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE_REPOSITORY , OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE_TAG , OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE_DIGEST , OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE (fully qualified reference) Why it exists. The prepare script writes an extra-resources/server/compose.yml that pulls the server image by name so packaged app installs do not need to build the container locally. User-visible behavior. With no environment overrides, packaging pulls ghcr.io/chenglabresearch/ouroboros-server:v<appVersion> . A release that has not yet published a matching image tag will fail at first startup with a docker pull error. When to reconsider. Set OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE_DIGEST to pin a specific build for a release, or point OUROBOROS_SERVER_IMAGE at a private registry for internal builds. Preinstalled plugin pins Symbol: productionPluginPins Value: neuroglancer.tag = v1.1.1 neuroglancer.artifact = neuroglancer-plugin-v1.1.1.zip autoseg.tag = v0.4.0-beta.2 autoseg.cpuArtifact = auto-segmentation-v0.4.0-beta.2-cpu.zip autoseg.cudaArtifact = auto-segmentation-v0.4.0-beta.2-cuda.zip Source: scripts/prepare-package-flavor.mjs lines 7-16 Environment overrides: OUROBOROS_NEUROGLANCER_PLUGIN_TAG , OUROBOROS_NEUROGLANCER_PLUGIN_ARTIFACT , OUROBOROS_AUTOSEG_PLUGIN_TAG , OUROBOROS_AUTOSEG_CPU_PLUGIN_ARTIFACT , OUROBOROS_AUTOSEG_CUDA_PLUGIN_ARTIFACT Why it exists. These are the exact plugin release versions that the with-plugins-cpu and with-plugins-cuda package flavors ship. The core flavor ships no preinstalled plugins. User-visible behavior. A packaged app pins the listed plugin versions in extra-resources/preinstalled-plugins/ . First launch copies each into the user's plugin folder if the installed version is older or missing. Bump workflow. productionPluginPins and the fallback neuroglancerArtifactForTag / autosegArtifactForTag builders in scripts/prepare-package-flavor.mjs move together on every plugin release. The single-file edit lives in scripts/prepare-package-flavor.mjs : update the tags in productionPluginPins , and the fallback builders pick up the new filename shape automatically. The environment overrides above take precedence over both. When to reconsider. Update these pins whenever a new upstream plugin release becomes the intended default. Bump both the tag and the artifact filename together, since the artifact filename embeds the tag. Where the values come from Every value above was read directly from the tree at the time this page was written. The remaining file explorer constants live together as a block at the top of src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts ; the shared teardown delay lives in src/shared/constants.ts so both the main process and the renderer import the same value. If you edit any of them, update this page in the same commit so operators and plugin authors can rely on it.
